title: Signatures of symmetry-stabilized Dirac fermions in correlated oxide CaNbO3 thin films
authors: Yunkyu Park, Seoung-Hun Kang, Jeongkeun Song, Minsik Kong, Seohee Kim, Shan Lin, Eun Sang Choi, Km Rubi, Hua Zhou, Sangmoon Yoon, Hu Miao, Satoshi Okamoto, Jong Mok Ok, Ho Nyung Lee
abstract: Symmetry-protected electronic states in correlated oxides offer a route to combining topology, lattice tunability, and many-body interactions, but creating such topological electronic states in complex oxides remains challenging. Here, we show that oxygen octahedral rotations provide a symmetry-control parameter for stabilizing Dirac-related electronic states in epitaxial CaNbO3 films. By comparing compressively strained tetragonal films and relaxed orthorhombic films, we demonstrate that distinct octahedral rotation patterns preserve nonsymmorphic symmetry and lead to distinct transport signatures consistent with Dirac-like electronic states. The films exhibit metallic transport with high mobility of 138,000 cm2 V-1 s-1, multichannel conduction, and Shubnikov-de Haas oscillations from small high-mobility Fermi pockets. Landau-fan diagram analysis indicates finite Berry-phase contributions, while first-principles calculations reveal a strain-driven evolution from nodal-line band crossings in the orthorhombic phase to Dirac-electron band features in the tetragonal phase. These results establish oxygen octahedral symmetry as a design knob for engineering topological electronic states in correlated perovskite oxides.
summary: This work demonstrates that oxygen octahedral rotations in $	ext{CaNbO}_3$ thin films act as a structural mechanism to control electronic topology. By comparing strained (tetragonal) and relaxed (orthorhombic) films, the authors link specific crystal symmetries to distinct electronic states, such as Dirac fermions or nodal lines. This establishes a powerful design principle for engineering topological materials in correlated oxides.
main_problem: The study addresses the challenge of stabilizing and characterizing symmetry-protected Dirac-related electronic states in complex, correlated oxide thin films.
main_result: Oxygen octahedral rotations act as a structural design knob, allowing the engineering of distinct topological electronic states—Dirac crossings in the tetragonal phase and nodal lines in the orthorhombic phase—in $	ext{CaNbO}_3$.
method: The research combines epitaxial thin-film growth (PLD) with comprehensive transport measurements (magnetotransport, Hall effect) and first-principles DFT calculations.
model_or_system: The physical system is epitaxial $	ext{CaNbO}_3$ thin films grown on $	ext{SrTiO}_3$ substrates, where the electronic structure is controlled by strain-induced changes in oxygen octahedral rotations (OORs) between tetragonal and orthorhombic phases.
key_observables: Ultrahigh electron mobility ($\mu \approx 138,000 	ext{ cm}^2	ext{V}^{-1}	ext{s}^{-1}$), Shubnikov-de Haas (SdH) oscillations, and the evolution of band crossings from nodal lines to Dirac points.
important_parameters: Compressive strain, oxygen octahedral rotation patterns ($a^0a^0c^-$ vs $a^+b^-b^-$), and temperature/magnetic field regimes for quantum transport measurements.
main_assumptions: The electronic properties are primarily governed by the symmetry constraints imposed by the octahedral rotations, which dictate the topological nature of the band structure.
figures_summary: Figures summarize the strain-driven evolution of OOR symmetry and associated electronic topology, showing structural characterization (RHEED, XRD), transport measurements ($ho(T)$, mobility), and quantum oscillation data (SdH oscillations) for both strained and relaxed films.
paper_structure: The paper follows a structure comparing two distinct structural phases (strained tetragonal vs. relaxed orthorhombic), using structural characterization to define the symmetry, followed by transport measurements to confirm the resulting electronic signatures (Dirac vs. nodal lines), all underpinned by DFT calculations.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state physics, the concept of using structural degrees of freedom (OORs) to engineer topological electronic states is highly relevant to designing quantum materials for quantum computing applications.
